title: Preach always
hook: Franciscans are known for serving before speaking

segments.voice: Yesterday, a prayer that carries Francis's spirit, asking to be made into a tool in someone else's hands. Your line was an instrument of peace. Where did you get to be one, even for a minute? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-two.

A rule for a band of brothers has a chapter on preaching. It opens with a warning: no brother is to preach against the Church's ways, or without his minister's permission. So far, a rule about who may stand up and speak. Then comes one short line that widens the whole chapter: all the brothers, though, should preach by their works. Not some of them. All of them. The cook, the one mending a roof, the one sitting up with a sick man. The rule is the one Francis of Assisi gave his first brothers, and in that line nobody is left out of preaching. Today's word is a phrase. Preach always.

Francis didn't invent the idea. He found it in the Gospel. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says: "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven." Notice who gets the glory. Not the one shining. The light points away from itself. Then the letter of James puts it with a shrug: "shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works." Words can say faith. Works show it. And the first letter of John says it tenderly: "My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth." That's the ground Francis stood on. In the stories told about him and his first brothers, they work with their hands, they look after lepers, they sweep out churches. When they do speak, the speaking comes out of a life people have already watched. Now, a fair word for the other side of it. The early stories about Francis have him preaching out loud too, in town squares as well as churches. And Paul asks how anyone will believe in one of whom they have not heard. So, in this way of reading it, it isn't works instead of words. It's an order of things. The life comes first and stays longest. Words, when they come, have somewhere to stand. A sermon ends. A life is preached every day, including the days you'd rather nobody was watching.
screen: `SHEW ME THY FAITH BY MY WORKS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one act of service you'll do today without saying a word about it. Sit and breathe. Let someone come to mind who could use a hand: a tired coworker, a neighbor, someone at home. Now find one small thing. Wash the thing they'd have to wash. Refill what's empty. Carry what's heavy. Then decide the harder part: you won't mention it. No hint, no credit. If you pray, you can offer it to God in advance. The bell holds the time.
Preach always. The heart of a line in Francis's rule: let all the brothers preach by their works, so the life speaks before the mouth does.
Your line: preach with your life. Today, do the one wordless thing you chose, and let it stay wordless, even if nobody ever finds out. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Franciscan friars and sisters, and lay people who follow Francis's way, often serve the poor and the sick in quiet, practical ways, and speak of letting their lives bear witness alongside their words.

myth: Francis's rule asks only the brothers with permission to preach by their works
permission is for preaching in words. preaching by works is asked of all the brothers.
the early stories say Francis never preached out loud
they have him preaching aloud, in town squares too. the point is the order: the life first, then the words.
in Matthew, the light points glory away from the one shining
they see your good works and glorify your Father which is in heaven.

fork.setup: you're one of Francis's first brothers. you'll never stand in a pulpit. what does the rule ask of you?
options: nothing; preaching is for the ones with permission.
preach by your works, like all the brothers.
argue with people in the square until they agree.
fork.reveal: the rule asks all the brothers to preach by their works. the ones who never spoke in church were still preachers.

original.note: Greek: to proclaim aloud, as a herald does; Mark 16:15 uses this verb for preach the gospel.

trapdoor: what you thought: preaching means a sermon from a pulpit.
what it means: in Francis's rule, every brother preaches, and the life preaches first.
what a scholar hears: Earlier Rule ch. 17 limits who may preach in words, then asks all the brothers to preach by their works.

sources.ref: Francis of Assisi, Earlier Rule (Regula non bullata), ch. 17

notes: Claims rule: the statement that 'preach the gospel at all times; when necessary use words' does not appear in Francis's extant writings is a negative manuscript claim; it is widely noted by Franciscan scholars but confirm the phrasing 'as we have them'.
Earlier Rule ch. 17 paraphrased ('all the brothers should preach by their works', Latin 'omnes tamen fratres operibus praedicent'); confirm chapter and wording.
Hook: 'after a warning about who may preach in church' summarizes the opening of ch. 17 (no brother to preach contrary to the Church's form or without permission); confirm.
Teach: 'they look after lepers, they sweep out churches' draws on the early Franciscan sources (Testament, early lives); confirm these are fair as 'stories told about him'.
Paul (Romans 10:14) paraphrased for the need for words.
Original: κηρύσσω and its use (κηρύξατε) in Mark 16:15; confirm accent and pronunciation.

Editor (2026-10-02): hook rewritten to open on Earlier Rule ch. 17 itself and to drop the misattributed 'use words if necessary' angle, which repeated day 1131's 'prayer wrongly credited to Francis' hook and rested on a negative manuscript claim; myth, trapdoor and word line updated to match. 'Francis preached out loud, often' softened to what the early stories say (Celano added to sources); the narrator's 'the good news still has to be said plainly' (belief-pushing) cut. The first review note about the misattributed saying no longer applies.
